source_text: Tu igitur, ut omnia, profanissime effatus es, in Christi carne non fuisse quod humanae naturae est; quod certe de nulla Scripturae rationabilis vena, sed de solo Manichaeorum coeno deceptus hausisti. Verum ut maior copia defendendae veritatis appareat, concedamus te somniasse, in Christo carnis quam dicis concupiscentiam non fuisse; quod certe in Manichaei prius, postea in Apollinaris furore damnatum est; tuo tamen quid possit dogmati suffragari; cum non continuo sequeretur malum esse, si quid ille assumere noluisset? Quoniam gradatim crescentibus meritis bonorum, diceretur isse per optima, nec bona tamen infra se locata superiorum electione damnasse. Quomodo enim nuptias non infamavit, integritatem secutus; ita nec sensum carnis genitalis damnasset, si eius possibilitatem nec in substantia sua habere voluisset.
pass_a_gloss: You therefore, as in all things, have spoken most profanely, that what belongs to human nature was not in Christ's flesh; which certainly you, deceived, drew from no vein of reasonable Scripture, but from the filth of the Manichaeans alone. But that a greater plenty of defending the truth may appear, let us grant that you dreamed that the desire of the flesh which you name was not in Christ; which certainly was condemned first in the fury of Manichaeus, afterward in that of Apollinaris; yet what could it support for your dogma; since it would not immediately follow that something was evil if he had been unwilling to assume it? Because, the deserts of goods growing by steps, it would be said that he had gone through the best things, and nevertheless had not condemned the goods placed below him by the choice of higher things. For as he did not infame marriages, having followed integrity; so he would not have condemned the sense of genital flesh, if he had not wanted to have its possibility even in his own substance.

pass_b_english: So here, as in everything, you have spoken most profanely in saying that what belongs to human nature was absent from Christ’s flesh. You drew this, deceived, not from any sound vein of Scripture but solely from Manichaean filth. Yet to display a greater abundance of resources for defending truth, let us grant your dream that the desire of the flesh you speak of was absent from Christ. This was certainly condemned first in Manichaean and afterward in Apollinarist frenzy. But what support could it give your doctrine? It would not immediately follow that something was evil if he had chosen not to assume it. Since good things rise by degrees in worth, one could say that he proceeded through the best without condemning goods placed below him by choosing those above. Just as he did not defame marriage by following virginity, so he would not have condemned the sensation of the reproductive flesh even if he had been unwilling to possess its capacity in his own substance.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
